evidence.section_title: A Combined Cognitive–Behavioral Family Education Intervention for Depression in Children: A Treatment Development Study
evidence.quote: [/page/0/Text/3] This study evaluates the acceptability and efficacy of a combined cognitive—behavioral family education intervention for fourth through sixth graders reporting depressive symptoms.

[page/1/Text/3] To address these limitations in the literature, we developed a 10-session combined cognitive–behavioral and family education intervention for children. The intervention included three distinct features. First, the intervention included a family education session designed to promote generalization of skills to key environmental contexts (home, school, community), encourage parents to support the learning that was achieved through the group sessions, and foster positive attitudes towards the skills emphasized in the intervention. Second, consistent with Meichenbaum and Biemiller's emphasis on the importance of increasing levels of self-direction in moving from skill acquisition to mastery in CBT interventions (Meichenbaum & Biemiller; 1998), the intervention was designed to address the progression from skill acquisition, to skill consolidation (through practice), to assuming a consulting or teaching role. Intervention sessions were structured around the development of a videotape by the children, which was shown to parents at "family night," and provided multiple opportunities for children to practice and consolidate the skills introduced in each CBT session. During family night each child then assumed the role of "consultant" as they taught their parents the skills emphasized in the group session. Finally, to address the high rate of comorbid symptoms/disorders and adjustment problems observed among youth with depression, the intervention included generic CBT components such as problem-solving and social skills training as well as depression-specific CBT components similar to those included in other cognitive–behavioral interventions for depression (Clarke et al., 1999; Lewinsohn, Clarke, Hops, & Andrews, 1990).

[/page/3/Text/9] Items included in this report focused on (1) child and parent ratings of the how helpful the group was, (2) parent reports of whether they would have liked more family sessions, and (3) parent reports of whether they noticed their children talking about or using the skills taught in the group (e.g., problem-solving, taking their emotional temperature, setting personal goals, relaxation, stopping negative thoughts, saying positive things to others, and planning fun activities).

[/page/4/Text/3] The intervention had three distinct components: (1) the inclusion of a family education component designed to enhance generalization to real world settings and promote a supportive family environment, (2) the development by the children of a videotape that was shown to the parents during the family education session in which children demonstrated and practiced the skills introduced during each CBT session, and (3) the inclusion of both generic and depression-specific CBT components to provide a means of targeting processes associated with depression as well as processes associated with frequent comorbid symptoms/disorders or life problems or both.
[/page/6/Text/3] These findings are consistent with the prediction that the intervention would be successful in decreasing negative cognitive patterns and enhancing coping skills.
[page/6/Text/6] Results of this study provide preliminary support for the efficacy of our combined CBT family education intervention.
[/page/2/Text/5] The sample included 15 girls and 8 boys

[/page/2/Text/5] Eligibility for study participation was based on a screening for self-reported depressive symptoms with the use of the Children's Depression Inventory (CDI). From an initial sample of 88 children, 23 children were selected to participate in the study on the basis of the following criteria: (1) a total CDI score of 8 or above and (2) parents consented and children assented to study participation. [/page/2/Text/6] On the basis of responses to the CDI items, algorithms were generated to match the DSM-IV criteria for major depression and dysthymic disorder. Using these algorithms, children were tentatively classified as meeting probable criteria for major depression (endorsed five-criterion depressive symptoms including depressed/irritable mood or anhedonia) and dysthymia/minor depression (endorsed three-criterion symptoms including depressed/irritable mood or anhedonia). Because the CDI assesses current state and does not include questions on duration of dysphoric mood, these algorithms should be viewed as identifying children who endorsed a sufficient number of core depressive symptoms as specified by DSM-IV but for whom the duration criteria was uncertain. Of the 23 children participating in the intervention phase of the project, 11 children (47.8%) met tentative criteria for major depression. Another 9 children (39%) met tentative criteria for minor depression/dysthymia (dysphoric mood plus two ancillary symptoms).
